entry.title: Over sky, under ground & down the beamline: The pursuit of WIMP dark matter presented by Linda Xu

media:group.media:title: Over sky, under ground & down the beamline: The pursuit of WIMP dark matter presented by Linda Xu
Milky Way Dark Matter Simulation
media:group.media:description:
Darkness surrounds us.
A structure of dark matter envelopes our Milky Way galaxy.
Gravity makes the dark matter clump together and form dense structures, referred to as halos (bright areas in this simulation). Galaxies are thought to form inside these halos. SLAC and Stanford researchers used measurements of faint satellite galaxies orbiting the Milky Way to derive limits on how often dark matter particles can possibly collide with regular matter particles, and simulated the formation of the dark matter structure surrounding the Milky Way from the early universe to today.
Credit: SLAC/Stanford University/Ethan Nadler/Risa Wechsler/R. Kaehler

entry.title: Has dark matter been detected? Physicists explain mystery event

media:group.media:title: Has dark matter been detected? Physicists explain mystery event
media:group.media:description:
Has dark matter finally been detected? In 2026, the LZ experiment reported a single event that did not match any known source of ordinary events. SLAC scientists Dan Akerib and Tom Shutt, who have spent their careers hunting dark matter, explain what they saw, how scientists check every event and why the window for this search is closing.
Most of the matter in the universe is invisible. We see its gravitational effects, but no one knows what it is. LZ (LUX-ZEPLIN) is one of the most sensitive experiments ever built to catch it. Nearly a mile underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, South Dakota, LZ holds a tank of liquid xenon that gives off a flash of light when a particle hits one of its atoms.
Scientists say it’s too early to call it a discovery. More data will tell whether it was dark matter or an unusual background (an ordinary event that can mimic dark matter).
LZ is an international collaboration of about 250 scientists and engineers, managed by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. SLAC developed LZ’s xenon purification systems and custom electrodes, and contributes to its operations and data analysis.
Read more: https://www6.slac.stanford.edu/news/2026-09-01-lz-sees-surprising-result-search-dark-matter LZ experiment: https://lz.lbl.gov
Producer & writer: Olivier Bonin Story editor: Ali Sundermier Featuring: Dan Akerib, Tom Shutt Voice-over: Kathryn Olsen LZ tank animation: Greg Stewart LZ footage: Nick Hubbard / Sanford Underground Research Facility Plot and table: 2026 LZ Collaboration paper Music: Waiting by KV https://youtube.com/c/KVmusicprod
SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory explores how the universe works at the biggest, smallest and fastest scales and invents powerful tools used by researchers around the globe. SLAC is operated by Stanford University for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science.

media:group.media:description:
Dark matter, that unseen stuff currently detectible only by its gravitational influence on other matter, can warp and distort our view of the universe. Studying the effects of dark matter allows astrophysicists to simulate different times in the history of the universe and to render these simulations into high-definition video.
Scientists from the Kavli Institute for Particle Astrophysics and Cosmology, located at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory and Stanford University, did just that for the Hayden Planetarium.

entry.title: How we capture attosecond science: Part II

media:group.media:title: How we capture attosecond science: Part II
media:group.media:description:
How do you capture attosecond science?
An attosecond is one billionth of a billionth of a second. It's how fast electrons move. So, in order to capture electron motion, scientists need a camera with a shutter speed on an attosecond timescale, and it took decades to create that tool. That tool is the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS) - the world's most powerful X-ray laser - and it's here at SLAC.
LCLS can produce pulses of light that are just a few attoseconds long, effectively freezing the motion of electrons in time and is enabling us to study the fastest processes in nature at the heart of chemical reactions.

entry.title: What will our 3.2 billion-pixel camera help us see?

media:group.media:title: What will our 3.2 billion-pixel camera help us see?
media:group.media:description:
The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory surveys the southern sky from Chile with the LSST Camera, the largest digital camera ever built for astronomy, built at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. Every night, 700 images are instantly transmitted to the Rubin U.S. Data Facility at SLAC, where computers compare them with earlier images to spot supernovae, asteroids and flaring stars, and send alerts to scientists around the world. Over its 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time, Rubin will also offer clues about dark matter and dark energy, which make up 95% of the universe. We're celebrating #Freedom250 and beyond by showing how SLAC helps answer the biggest questions about our universe.

entry.title: A path towards the self-driving laboratory

media:group.media:title: A path towards the self-driving laboratory
media:group.media:description:
Enter the self-driving lab
SLAC researchers are leading a new project for autonomous labs where SI agents, robots and intelligent detectors work together to run experiments end to end. SI agents can interpret experimental data and direct robotic arms and other subsystems to make delicate adjustments to samples and X-ray beams, at the same time as filtering the most valuable results for processing and analysis so that researchers can walk away from their experiments with immediate insights instead of a mountain of raw data to sift through.
Working with Stanford, UChicago, industry and national labs including Argonne, Brookhaven and Berkeley labs, the team is designing systems meant to translate across the DOE’s entire network of scientific facilities.

entry.title: SLAC Public Lecture | Blazing the path to a fusion future presented by Arianna Gleason

media:group.media:title: SLAC Public Lecture | Blazing the path to a fusion future presented by Arianna Gleason
media:group.media:description:
Realizing usable electrical power from nuclear fusion has been a grand challenge for physicists and engineers for more than 70 years. Recently the National Ignition Facility (NIF) at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory has made a major step forward, realizing multi-megajoule energy yield from tiny pellets containing deuterium and tritium compressed by the action of powerful lasers. The next step is to make the compression to a fusion plasma smoother and more robust. Here at SLAC, our free-electron X-ray laser LCLS gives us a unique instrument to visualize the compression process, both dynamically on the pellet materials and chemically at the atomic scale. Our program is leveraging detailed, AI-driven simulations. In this lecture, I will describe our experiments, which operate on ultra-fast timescales and at ultra-high pressures, to smooth the path to commercial fusion energy.
About the Speaker: Arianna Gleason received her PhD in earth and planetary science from the University of California, Berkeley, in 2010. After a postdoctoral appointment at Stanford University, she worked at Los Alamos National Laboratory in the shock and detonation physics group. She joined SLAC in 2018 as a staff scientist. Her passion is visualizing the behavior and response of materials at atomic-scales in the most extreme environments possible in nature – from planetary cores to stellar interiors. This allows her to uncover nature’s secrets of high-pressure mineral physics and planetary evolution from the atomic level up. In 2019, she received the Department of Energy Office of Science Early Career Award in fusion energy science and the United States federal government Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE) in 2025, as well as being nominated as a Fellow of the Mineralogical Society of America in 2025.
As Senior Scientist and Deputy Director of the High Energy Density Science Division at SLAC, Arianna leads programs on inertial fusion and seeks to lay the foundation to bring fusion power to our everyday lives.
Learn more about the SLAC public lectures here: https://www6.slac.stanford.edu/news-and-events/events/public-lectures

entry.title: How will Rubin Observatory map dark matter?

media:group.media:title: How will Rubin Observatory map dark matter?
media:group.media:description:
Risa Wechsler, astrophysicist explains: 85% of the matter in the universe is dark matter, a substance that interacts through gravity but doesn't emit light. The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory will enhance our understanding by mapping 20 billion galaxies across half the sky using gravitational lensing to pinpoint all matter, visible or not. Additionally, it will explore tiny galaxies with few stars but massive dark matter clumps, providing insights into dark matter's properties. Its comprehensive survey will potentially reveal clues about dark matter's particle and further elucidate the universe's structure and evolution.
Learn more at https://www6.slac.stanford.edu/research/slac-science-explained/lsst-camera

Quantum computing, fusion energy, and so much more. The world’s most powerful X-ray laser is here at SLAC and its getting upgraded.
